> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Youth psychopathology is a pressing global challenge.

High comorbidity rates and moderate psychotherapy effects highlight the need for transdiagnostic approaches, which target processes cutting across diagnostic categories to better understand the etiology and maintenance of mental disorders.

Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) enables to examine transdiagnostic processes in (almost) real-time in the natural environment of children and adolescents and therefore offers the opportunity to capture the micro-level, within-person dynamics through which psychopathology unfolds in everyday life.
However, transdiagnostic research in children and adolescents so far has seldomly incorporated EMA and EMA studies in youth have rarely adopted a transdiagnostic focus.

Although systematic reviews show that EMA is feasible in children and adolescents and can capture fluctuations, contexts, social interactions, and treatment-related change related to psychopathology, transdiagnostic EMA applications in youth remain limited.

This methodological perspective paper provides an overview of the advantages of integrating EMA into the methodological repertoire of transdiagnostic research and practice with children and adolescents.

We further provide recommendations on how to realize a transdiagnostic perspective using EMA with children and adolescents, summarize recent developments in this field, and outline key steps for the development and evaluation of a transdiagnostic EMA tool for youth.
Mental disorders in children and adolescents (hereafter: "youth") present a global societal challenge (McGorry et al., 2024).

text.text: Mental health research and treatment have traditionally been organized around disorder-specific diagnostic categories.

text.formatted: The integration of ecological momentary assessment (EMA) methods into transdiagnostic research offers one promising methodological approach to advance our understanding on the dynamic micro-processes through which psychopathology emerges and fluctuates in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Wichers, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Vize & Wright, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In this methodological perspective paper, we first provide a brief introduction to transdiagnostic approaches and the application of EMA in youth psychopathology.

We then discuss how integrating EMA into transdiagnostic research with youth may advance transdiagnostic conceptualization of psychopathology, increase our understanding of transdiagnostic processes, and inform the development and optimization of transdiagnostic treatments.
We summarize recent developments in transdiagnostic EMA research and outline important steps to realize the potential of a transdiagnostic EMA perspective in research and practice with youth.

The most common transdiagnostic conceptualizations to psychopathology comprise the network approach to psychopathology (Borsboom, 2017), the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP; Kotov et al., 2017), the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC; Insel et al., 2010), and the Clinical Staging Model (McGorry et al., 2006).

text.text: In brief, the network theory and related theories (e.g. dynamic complex systems theory; Borsboom, 2017; Robinaugh et al., 2019) conceptualize mental disorders as maladaptive patterns arising from causally interacting symptoms (or more broadly, biopsychosocial and environmental variables), rather than seeing symptoms as indicators of a common latent cause.

text.text: RDoC is a framework for conceptualizing mental disorders across core domains of neurobehavioral functioning considering various aspects of environment and units of analysis (e.g., genetics, physiology, self-report; Insel et al., 2010), and finally, Clinical Staging approaches combine a categorical and dimensional approach including different stages of disease progression (e.g., from asymptomatic/at risk to treatment resistance), with specific implications for the allocation of prevention and prognosis of mental disorders (Cosci & Fava, 2013; McGorry et al., 2006).

text.text: While the four approaches have developed rather independently from one another and differ in their conceptual foundations, they coincide on the basic premise that traditional categorical conceptualizations of mental disorders as formulated in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) and the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) do not fully capture the complexity of mental disorders.

These approaches also offer different accounts of the emergence and co-occurrence of mental disorders, while underscoring the importance of examining transdiagnostic (vs. disorder-specific) processes (Eaton et al., 2023; Rief et al., 2023).

text.text: This shared emphasis provides a strong rationale for methodological approaches capable of capturing transdiagnostic processes as they unfold over time.

However, much of the empirical research underlying transdiagnostic conceptualizations of psychopathology has relied on cross-sectional data and between-person differences in adults (Eaton et al., 2023), providing limited insight into the dynamic nature of psychopathology within youth over time (Vize & Wright, 2024).

text.text: It is useful to distinguish transdiagnostic factors that characterize differences between individuals and those that characterize differences within individuals over time.

The former includes environmental factors (e.g., early life adversity: Wade et al., 2022; socioeconomic status: Peverill et al., 2021), biological (e.g., genetic risk; Riglin et al., 2020), and psychological factors (e.g., temperament: Rettew et al., 2005; executive functioning: Yang et al., 2022) that can explain why some individuals are more vulnerable than others.

text.text: These can be distinguished from transdiagnostic factors that lie within individuals and can fluctuate or change with time.

Such within-person factors may include experiences and behaviors (and on a broader level 'symptoms', but see Guðmundsdóttir et al., 2026) that are shared across disorders (e.g., insomnia, difficulties concentrating, irritability; Forbes et al., 2023).

text.text: One very frequently empirically examined transdiagnostic process is emotion regulation: it has been shown that difficulties in emotion regulation are present across a wide range of mental disorders in youth (Kraft et al., 2023) and adults (Clamor et al., 2026).

text.text: In addition, methodological aspects limit our current understanding of transdiagnostic processes.

First, the majority of present research is based on instruments that ask youth and/or their caregivers to recall behaviors, cognitions, and feelings within a specified time frame (e.g., traditional questionnaires; Russell & Gajos, 2020).

text.text: Consequently, appropriate study designs and assessment methods need to be applied to elucidate how proposed transdiagnostic processes such as emotion regulation, stress responsivity, interoception, and reward processing (among others) unfold dynamically within individuals and across mental disorders.

Longitudinal research spanning weeks or months can capture longer-term processes and their associations with psychopathology, whereas examining subjective experiences and behaviors over periods of minutes and hours allows their short-term dynamics to be studied in everyday life.
This micro-level perspective may help identify the smallest "building blocks" through which psychopathology emerges and fluctuates (Wichers et al., 2014).

text.text: A shift from disorder-specific treatments, which target symptoms and mechanisms characteristic of individual mental disorders (e.g., exposure-based CBT for social anxiety disorder) to transdiagnostic treatments is currently underway, emphasizing commonalities and shared processes rather than differences between disorders (Schäuffele et al., 2021; Temkin et al., 2018).

text.text: While most of these treatments were developed for adults, some have been adapted or developed specifically for youth.

One of the earliest explicit transdiagnostic interventions for youth was the extension of the Unified Protocol for the Treatment of Emotional Disorders (UP, Barlow et al., 2004) to youth which aims to target transdiagnostic dimensions such as emotion awareness, cognitive reappraisal, tolerance and regulation of (negative) emotions through cognitive behavioral techniques (Ehrenreich et al., 2009; Ehrenreich-May et al., 2018).

text.text: In other transdiagnostic approaches, rather than emphasizing the identification of underlying processes common to several mental disorders, the focus lies on common elements interventions that are highly overlapping across evidence-based psychological treatments.

For instance, the Modular Approach to Therapy for Children (MATCH, Chorpita & Weisz, 2009), aims to select evidence-based treatment modules for individual patients based on clinical judgement, case formulation, patientcentered data assessments, or a combination thereof (Schäuffele et al., 2021).

Moreover, such information could also be a valuable additional source to help clinician's identify individualized treatment targets and to inform the selection or sequencing of treatment modules (Li et al., 2024).

text.text: Despite promising developments in transdiagnostic research across the past decades, important challenges remain, including the dynamic expression of psychopathology across time and developmental stages in youth, accounting for individual differences in symptom expression, understanding how transdiagnostic processes unfold dynamically and within individuals in everyday life, and identifying which of these represent meaningful and changeable treatment targets (Vize & Wright, 2023; Dalgleish et al., 2020).

text.text: We argue that EMA offers a valuable complementary approach to addressing these challenges.

text.text: Several aspects need to be considered when implementing EMA, particularly in youth populations.
First, protocols should minimize participant burden and facilitate compliance.
Therefore, prompts should be brief and fast to respond (Eisele et al., 2022) and sampling schedules should be compatible with adolescents' daily routines (e.g., awakening, bedtime, school hours).

text.text: In clinical populations, repeated assessment also raises safety considerations, particularly when EMA assesses potentially acute risks such as suicidality.

Although perceived burden and negative emotional reactions to repeated assessments of suicidal ideation seems to be low in general, a minority of individuals has reported increased negative feelings or suicidal thoughts in previous studies (Kivelä et al., 2022; Lühr et al., 2026).

text.text: Therefore, safety protocols should be installed that may include clearly defined safety measures for responding to concerning reports, such as provision of emergency contacts or real-time alerts to researchers or clinicians (Kivelä et al., 2022).

text.text: Next, developmental differences represent a further important aspect.

Youth differ substantially in cognitive abilities, reading comprehension, and capacity to report on internal experiences, making age-appropriate measurement particularly important (Wolley et al., 2004).

text.text: From a methodological perspective, EMA measures of specific psychological constructs often comprise single or several few items and this brevity, together with the dynamic nature inherent to the constructs and their assessment in real life presents unique challenges to the psychometric evaluation of reliability and validity (Löchner et al., 2026).

text.text: Recent studies have begun to systematically evaluate the reliability and validity of youth-specific EMA measures, including momentary anxiety (Byrne et al., 2023), irritability (Hansen et al., 2025), rumination (Webb et al., 2025), and well-being (Buzzi et al., 2025; Kral et al., 2026).

text.text: Together, these studies suggest an emerging shift toward more systematic attention to the measurement quality and item standardization of EMA research.
Finally, EMA data can be analysed at different levels depending on the research questions.

When data from multiple individuals are collected, associations within individuals, between individuals, and whether within-person associations differ systematically between individuals can be examined.

Such analyses require statistical techniques that account for the nested structure of EMA data (e.g., observations nested within individuals), and interested readers are referred to Bolger and Laurenceau (2013) for further guidance (see also Revol et al., 2024 for data preprocessing).

text.text: Furthermore, EMA in individual patients can be used to identify person-specific ('idiographic') patterns of experiences and behaviors with a high temporal resolution and thereby inform clinical conceptualization and practice (Fisher et al., 2016; Mink et al., 2025; Piccirillo et al., 2026; Piccirillo et al., 2019).

text.text: Since research has not yet established a consensus on how individual treatment targets can be most reliably identified (e.g., Bastiaansen et al., 2020), further methodological work is needed to address this topic.

text.text: Importantly, although EMA can characterize temporal dynamics, observational intensive longitudinal data are neither necessary nor sufficient to establish causal effects; rather causal inference requires a clearly specified causal question and a study design that allows causal effects to be distinguished from alternative explanations (Rohrer & Murayama, 2023).

text.text: Randomized controlled trials and laboratory experiments can provide such evidence by experimentally manipulating the factor(s) of interest, while integrating EMA can reveal whether and how relevant findings on transdiagnostic processes generalize to within-person associations in naturalistic contexts (Crawford et al., 2022; Miller-Chagnon et al., 2024).

text.text: In addition, experimental manipulation can be embedded directly within intensive longitudinal designs.
Such 'microrandomized trials' can provide tests of within-person causal effects (Klasnja et al., 2015; Schmiedek & Neubauer, 2020; Neubauer et al., 2025).

text.text: Overall, EMA offers a unique opportunity to complement established transdiagnostic approaches by capturing the micro-level, within-person dynamics through which psychopathology unfolds in everyday life (Wichers, 2014).

text.text: Combining traditional assessment methods in transdiagnostic research (e.g., questionnaires, clinical interviews, experimental tasks, biological assessments) with EMA can capture complementary facets of phenomena across levels of analysis and help link transdiagnostic processes identified in laboratory or longer-term longitudinal research to their temporal and contextual expression in everyday life.
In youth, this may be particularly valuable because ongoing developmental changes may contribute to greater variability in emotions and cognitions (Bailen et al., 2018; Reitsema et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In youth, this may be particularly valuable because ongoing developmental changes may contribute to greater variability in emotions and cognitions <ref type="bibr">(Bailen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Reitsema et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, for network approaches, EMA provides a high temporal resolution of psychopathology-relevant experiences and behaviors such as negative affect, irritability, rumination, avoidance, and social withdrawal, and allows to examine whether these dynamically influence one another (e.g., Roefs et al., 2022; Wichers, 2014).

text.text: For RDoC, EMA may capture the real-world expression of domains (e.g., negative/positive valence systems, social processes, arousal systems), particularly when combined with behavioral or physiological measures (Naim et al., 2021; Raugh et al., 2019).

text.text: EMA may help clarify whether proposed transdiagnostic processes are consistently involved across mental disorders and whether their role varies across individuals, developmental stages, and contexts.

This is particularly relevant to developmental psychopathology, where the same underlying processes may contribute to different outcomes across development and where psychopathology can follow heterogeneous trajectories (Nolen-Hoeksema & Watkins, 2011; Tackett & Hallquist, 2022).

text.text: Combined with longer-term longitudinal designs, measurementburst approaches (i.e., repeated periods of EMA embedded within longer-term follow-ups), can link fine-grained within-person dynamics to longer-term intraindividual change (Chiang & Lam, 2020; Sliwinski, 2008).

text.text: Finally, EMA can benefit transdiagnostic treatments by facilitating the selection of individualized and contextually sensitive interventions and by monitoring processes of change in daily life (Fisher et al., 2016; Mink et al., 2025), although future research will need to establish how EMA-derived information can be most effectively integrated into treatment decision-making.

text.text: Previous EMA research into youth psychopathology has some shortcomings that prevent a transdiagnostic perspective on youth psychopathology.
First, the majority of EMA studies focused on a narrow range of constructs.

text.text: We reviewed all included studies (k = 50), extracted the reported items manually and grouped them into 22 distinct categories.
Across studies, negative (66%, 33/50) and positive (46%, 23/50) affect were assessed most frequently across studies.
In addition, several studies included items on contextual information such as social context (36%, 18/50), current activity (28%, 14/50), location (26%, 13/50).

Other experiences or behaviors relevant across youth mental disorders were underexamined in the included EMA-studies (e.g., emotion regulation/coping (26%, 13/50); sleep (6%, 3/50); Gregory & Sadeh, 2012).

text.text: Although comorbidity has been reported in several of these studies, observed phenomena from daily life were not examined or discussed as potentially relevant in relation to comorbidity.

In contrast, recent EMA studies in samples of late adolescents and young adults from the general population found dynamics of negative affect (e.g., variability and persistence of emotions) (Zhu et al., 2024), repetitive negative thinking (i.e., recurrent thinking process focused on negative content) (Funk et al., 2025), and stress responsivity (Speyer et al., 2023; Vaessen et al., 2017) as correlates or predictors for a range of (co-occurring) psychopathology, including depressive, anxiety, aggression, and ADHD symptoms.

text.text: It remains to be examined whether these findings generalize to younger age groups with full-blown (comorbid) mental disorders.

Third, from an analytical perspective, many prior EMA studies in youth psychopathology have primarily adopted a descriptive focus in that they merely investigated temporal fluctuations or frequencies of occurrences of symptoms without systematically linking symptoms to contextual antecedents or consequences (Thunnissen et al., 2022).

text.text: A purely descriptive focus overlooks EMA's unique potential in explaining psychopathology as it unfolds in daily life (Vize & Wright, 2024).

text.text: For instance, an interpersonal conflict (context) may be followed by momentarily increased negative affect, which, in turn, could increase the likelihood for non-suicidal self-injury in some adolescents and higher depressive mood in others (outcomes).
Person-level factors (e.g. internalizing symptomatology, personality facets) could potentially explain such interindividual differences in the within-person processes.

Statistical techniques are available to model such complex interrelations across the momentand person-level (e.g., multilevel regression, multilevel structural equation modelling ; Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013; Briganti et al., 2024; Sadikaj et al., 2021).

text.text: Yet, to date, only few studies have started to unravel such transdiagnostic processes using EMA and appropriate statistical techniques in youth with (comorbid) mental health problems (Thunnissen et al., 2022; see f.ex. Byrd et al., 2025; Tseng et al., 2023 for exceptions).

text.text: Fourth, EMA with youth has been applied mostly in research contexts, with very little translation into clinical practice (Kooiman et al., 2023).

text.text: Yet integrating EMA into routine assessment could bridge the science-practice gap by providing individualized, contextsensitive insights that inform treatment planning (Hofmann & Hayes, 2024).

text.text: A transdiagnostic EMA approach is particularly valuable in this regard, as it enables clinicians to monitor experiences and behaviors together with their situational embeddings across diagnostic boundaries, thereby avoiding the need to design separate EMA protocols for each disorder and providing a more efficient and clinically relevant picture of patients' difficulties.

This process-based information can highlight within-person processes that maintain comorbid mental problems, guide treatment selection, and help tailor interventions to the patient's needs (Hofmann & Hayes, 2024).

text.text: There is a lack of comprehensive EMA tools that capture key transdiagnostic experiences and behaviors in the daily lives of youth with psychopathology.
Most existing studies are descriptive, overlooking EMA's unique potential to reveal how psychopathology unfolds in real time.

A transdiagnostic EMA approach can monitor processes across diagnostic boundaries, and we argue that its adoption is a crucial next step for improving understanding and treatment of youth psychopathology.
Several large-scale projects have developed and evaluated transdiagnostic EMA tools, although the vast majority of research has focused on adults.

Although most authors did not explicitly position their work as transdiagnostic research, they assessed constructs relevant across mental disorders, including mood/affect, social interactions, sleep, and emotion regulation, and some included customizable items tailored to patient needs (e.g., Bos et al., 2022; Scholten et al., 2024), highlighting the potential of EMA to combine standardized assessment with personalization.

text.text: Taken together, the above-mentioned studies illustrate the growing interest in applying EMA to capture experiences and behaviors across mental health problems in daily life and to inform personalized assessment and treatment recommendations.
However, there is currently a focus on (young) adult populations.

Existing measurements for adults cannot be simply applied to youth populations due to developmental differences in cognitive, emotional, and social functioning, as well as variations in symptom presentation and expression across age groups (Steinberg, 2005).

text.text: A transdiagnostic EMA tool for youth should be able to assess theoretically and empirically supported experiences and behaviors that fluctuate from moment-to-moment or day-to-day and are relevant across youth mental disorders.
Even in the absence of conclusive evidence regarding causal roles, initial item sets can be derived from the literature and refined through expert consensus.

text.text: From a research perspective, this may include recruiting youth presenting with a broad range of (comorbid) internalizing and externalizing psychopathology, applying a multimethod approach, combining complementary assessment methods, including EMA, and systematically examining research questions such as (1) how transdiagnostic conceptualizations of psychopathology and previously identified transdiagnostic processes are reflected across different assessment methods, (2) how these processes operate at the micro-level and across developmental stages, and (3) how these processes change in response to transdiagnostic treatments.

text.text: In line with the above-mentioned recommendations, this project aims to deliver a youth-tailored transdiagnostic EMA tool that captures dynamic transdiagnostic processes in daily life and advances both transdiagnostic research and clinical practice in youth psychopathology.

Overall, research on transdiagnostic frameworks, processes, and treatments in youth with mental disorders would greatly benefit from incorporating a dynamic and developmentally sensitive within-person perspective.
Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) provides a valuable methodological tool for realizing this perspective.
However, EMA research in youth has largely neglected a transdiagnostic perspective.
We therefore outlined which aspects need to be considered when implementing EMA into transdiagnostic research alongside current developments on transdiagnostic EMA tools.

We provided recommendations on steps that should be taken to advance a transdiagnostic EMA perspective in youth and highlighted potential research questions concerning how transdiagnostic processes are reflected across assessment methods, unfold at the micro-level and across development, and change in response to transdiagnostic treatments.

To conclude, integrating EMA within transdiagnostic research and clinical practice holds considerable promise for advancing our understanding of within-person processes that are shared across or differ between youth mental disorders, while supporting the development of more personalized transdiagnostic treatments (Hofmann & Hayes, 2024; Sauer-Zavala et al., 2017).
